extracted.intended_audience: teachers, students of education, and educational philosophers
extracted.subtask_description: Extracting evaluative criteria and methodological standards for curriculum, pedagogy, and aims of education as discussed in a chapter on educational philosophy (contrasting Hegelian, Lockean/formal-discipline, Herbartian, and recapitulation theories).

rubrics_metrics.name: Against institutional conformity — education should not be mere assimilation
rubrics_metrics.description: Conformity, not transformation, is the essence of education (Hegelian view): against institutions as they are, individuals have no spiritual rights; personal development consists in obedient assimilation of the spirit of existing institutions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anti-pattern: treating education as enforcement of existing institutions and social roles. Prefer approaches that allow individual development and transformation rather than simply reproducing institutional forms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Formal discipline — training of mental faculties by repeated exercise
rubrics_metrics.description: Education should aim at creation of specific powers (attention, memory, observation, abstraction, etc.) by direct and conscious exercises (Locke's/classic formal-discipline view): repeated graded practice refines and perfects these faculties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Includes the classic program of graded repetitions (like training muscles) and using subjects (e.g., mathematics) as vehicles for exercising faculties. Scoring/assessment implication: measure ease, efficiency, economy, promptness in tasks trained. The page also sets out substantial criticisms (see other entries) about the limits and fallacies of this theory.

rubrics_metrics.name: No abstract, general faculties — abilities are specific to subject matter
rubrics_metrics.description: There is no such thing as an ability to see or hear or remember in general; there is only the ability to see or hear or remember something.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implication for instruction: do not attempt to train abstract 'powers' apart from concrete subject matter. Training must be tied to the specific content and purposes in which the ability is to be used; otherwise claimed transfer is illusory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contextual/subject-matter specificity — train faculties within meaningful material
rubrics_metrics.description: The forms of powers (perceiving, retaining, recalling, associating, attending, etc.) are shaped by exercise upon material presented; subject matter determines the character of developed powers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select subject matter that aligns with desired abilities. Anti-pattern: rote drills (e.g., memorizing meaningless lists) that isolate form from meaning and social purpose. Prefer coordinated, meaningful tasks that integrate relevant stimuli and responses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Breadth and variability of activity produce 'general' education
rubrics_metrics.description: The more varied the stimuli and responses coordinated in an activity, the more generally available (broad, flexible) the acquired ability; monotonous uniform exercise yields narrow, non-transferable skill.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Favor varied, flexible tasks (games, problem-based activities) over uniform repetitive drills (gymnasium/pulley-weights analogy). Evaluate curricula by how widely they engage and integrate diverse factors of response.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transfer is limited — specialization reduces transferability
rubrics_metrics.description: The more specialized the reaction, the less generally available the training secured; apparent 'transfer' from narrow exercises to general powers is largely a myth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not assume practice on narrow tasks (e.g., isolated spelling drills) will produce broad intellectual capacities. Assessment should check for actual performance across varied contexts, not inferred transfer.

rubrics_metrics.name: Social criterion for subject-matter selection
rubrics_metrics.description: The criterion for what pupils should observe, recall, and judge must be social: select those things which make the person an effective, competent member of the group in which he is associated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Curriculum designers should choose content aligned with the social roles and purposes learners will occupy. Anti-pattern: training attention to irrelevant or meaningless stimuli (e.g., cracks on a wall).

rubrics_metrics.name: Education as formation by presentation (Herbartian steps: preparation, presentation, application)
rubrics_metrics.description: Herbartian method: education proceeds by instruction in the literal sense — building presentations (content) into the mind from without; methodical steps include preparation (calling up prior presentations), presentation (new subject matter), interaction, and application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical checklist for lesson planning: prepare learners' prior ideas, present new material in sequence related to previous content, then apply the new content to tasks. Evaluate teaching by fidelity to these steps and by sequencing that takes account of prior knowledge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conscious method and specification of teaching aims
rubrics_metrics.description: Teaching should be a conscious business with definite aims and procedures rather than routine, accidental practice; Herbart's contribution centers on making instruction methodical and specifiable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Teachers should define explicit aims, methods, and sequences. Anti-pattern: leaving instruction to tradition or casual inspiration without explicit method.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize native endowment (heredity) as a limit but not a determinant
rubrics_metrics.description: Heredity provides the original endowment of impulses and tendencies; education must take the being as he is and make best use of existing capacities, but heredity does not predetermine outcomes — environment and instruction shape development.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Initial assessment of native aptitudes is a necessary preliminary; design environments to utilize existing activities. Do not waste effort trying to make individuals into things they're not naturally fitted to become, but also do not treat heredity as an excuse to avoid instruction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use the past as resource, not as prescriptive pattern (critique of recapitulation theory)
rubrics_metrics.description: Reject recapitulation/retrospection that requires children to repeat past cultural stages; study of past products is valuable only insofar as it enters into and informs present life, not as a retrospective standard.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Curriculum should not be organized as a staged replay of historical cultural epochs. Instead, draw on past literatures and products when they illuminate or serve present problems; avoid making the past a rival to the present.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aim of education: capacity for continued learning (education as capacity for further education)
rubrics_metrics.description: The conception that the result of the educative process is capacity for further education (as opposed to mere preparation for some future duty, unfolding from within, or narrow training of faculties).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate programs by whether they leave learners able to learn independently and adaptively in new situations. Anti-patterns include curricula that focus solely on preparing for a fixed future role or rote transmission of facts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Training is selection and coordination of responses — build complex integrated responses
rubrics_metrics.description: True training consists in selecting from diffused responses those adapted to effective use of stimuli and in establishing coordination among visual, manual, motor, auditory, and affective responses (e.g., connecting sight, hand action, temperature reaction, and vocal labels).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design activities that coordinate multiple modalities and foster associative networks (e.g., linking perception, action, and language). Assess whether training produces integrated, context-sensitive responses rather than isolated reflexes.
